article.overview: A secondary ion mass spectrometer (SIMS) determines the elemental and isotopic composition of a solid by bombarding its surface with a focused beam of primary ions and measuring the mass of the secondary ions that the impact releases [3]. The technique is sensitive enough to measure very small amounts of water and other volatile elements in lunar volcanic glass, and it has been applied to such samples in laboratories on Earth [1][2]. Flight-proven SIMS hardware exists elsewhere in the Solar System: the COSIMA analyser flew on ESA's Rosetta spacecraft and analysed dust from comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko [3][4]. In the sources accessed for this article, however, no secondary ion mass spectrometer has been confirmed as flown, operating or formally planned for the Moon. A lunar surface SIMS has been proposed as a way to study solar-wind sputtering of the regolith [5], but that remains a concept. This article therefore covers a laboratory technique, a non-lunar flight instrument and a lunar concept, and keeps those three categories separate.
article.description:
In a SIMS measurement, a primary ion beam strikes the sample surface and removes a small volume of material. Some of the removed material leaves as charged secondary ions, which are extracted by an electric field, separated by mass and detected [3]. COSIMA measured the flight time of each secondary ion to an ion detector, because all secondary ions were accelerated to the same kinetic energy and lighter ions arrive sooner [3]. The laboratory instruments used in the lunar volatile studies instead collected negatively charged secondary ions and built images of selected masses across the analysed spot [1]. SIMS requires calibration against standards of known composition, because the measured ion signal must be converted into concentration [1]. Its main advantage for lunar science is sensitivity to hydrogen-bearing species and other volatiles at very low concentrations in very small volumes [1]. On the Moon, the most relevant secondary ions would be those released when solar-wind protons (H+) and helium ions (He++) strike the regolith [5]. Lunar water studies also have to separate indigenous water from water added by solar-wind implantation or laboratory contamination [1].

This entry describes the SIMS technique as a payload class. It is not the same as the mass spectrometers planned for lunar sample analysis in other packages. For example, the PROSPECT sample-analysis package uses an ion trap mass spectrometer and a magnetic sector mass spectrometer rather than SIMS [8].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of SIMS in lunar science is to measure volatile and trace elements at concentrations that other techniques cannot reach. Saal et al. used SIMS to measure H2O, CO2, F, S and Cl in Apollo volcanic glass beads. The authors state that the improved SIMS methods reduce detection limits for these species by up to two orders of magnitude compared with electron microprobe, FTIR and earlier SIMS instruments [1]. They used the results to argue that the Moon's interior may contain indigenous water and was not entirely depleted in highly volatile elements [1]. Hauri et al. applied a NanoSIMS ion microprobe to melt inclusions, which are pockets of magma sealed inside olivine crystals before eruption and therefore less affected by water loss during eruption [2]. Applications beyond lunar volatiles include in-situ analysis of comet dust. The COSIMA experiment aimed to determine the elemental and key isotopic composition of cometary grains, including their organic components and mineralogical classification [3]. A third application is the study of how solar-wind ions sputter secondary ions from lunar regolith, which is relevant to surface composition studies [5].
article.operating_principle: A SIMS payload has a primary ion source, a target holder for the sample, an extraction and mass-analysis section, and a detector with its electronics [3]. COSIMA's design used an indium ion source producing 115In+ ions at 8 keV in pulses of about 3 ns, with an overall beam width of about 50 µm FWHM [3]. Because all secondary ions were accelerated to the same kinetic energy, their time of flight to the detector depends on their mass, and the instrument builds a mass spectrum from those flight times [3]. The laboratory instruments in the Saal et al. study used a Cs+ primary beam of about 14 nA accelerated to 10 kV. They collected negatively charged secondary ions and monitored images of 12C, 17OH, 19F, 32S and 35Cl [1]. Each sample was pre-sputtered for 3 to 5 minutes before a measurement of about 10 minutes [1]. Quantification relied on standards: the authors plotted the known concentrations of standard materials against measured ratios of each volatile to 30Si [1]. A lunar SIMS would need its primary ion beam and mass analyser to operate in vacuum. This is general engineering reasoning, not a figure taken from a cited source.
article.scientific_importance: The scientific importance of SIMS for the Moon rests on the volatile budget of the lunar interior. Saal et al. note that evidence for indigenous water in lunar samples had remained elusive, consistent with the general view that the Moon is anhydrous, and they describe their results as the first evidence for indigenous water in the lunar interior [1]. Their modelled pre-eruptive water content is 745 ppm as a best estimate and at least 260 ppm at the 95% confidence level. These are model-derived values for the magma before eruption, not direct measurements [1]. Hauri et al. measured 615 to 1410 ppm water in olivine-hosted melt inclusions. Their abstract reports that earlier direct measurements of lunar volcanic glass had not exceeded about 50 ppm [2]. Taken together, the studies show that SIMS can resolve water contents in lunar materials well below the limits of older techniques. They also show that interpretation depends on sample selection and on how much water the magma lost during eruption [1][2]. For an in-situ lunar SIMS, the scientific value would lie in measuring volatiles and isotopes at a surface site rather than in returned samples. That is a motivation for such an instrument, not a demonstrated result.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for a secondary ion mass spectrometer. The sources accessed publish spacecraft-level figures only for COSIMA [3]. The laboratory instruments used in [1] and [2] are identified by model name, but their mass, dimensions and power are not stated in the sources accessed. The examples below are not directly comparable: a flown space instrument, laboratory analytical instruments and a proposed measurement concept serve different purposes and have different interfaces, so no comparison table is given.

examples.name: COSIMA (COmetary Secondary Ion Mass Analyser), ESA Rosetta orbiter
examples.type: Flown space instrument (comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko). Not a lunar instrument.
examples.status: Flown and operated at a comet [3][4].
examples.description: **Status: flown and operated at a comet, not on the Moon [3][4].** COSIMA was one of three cometary dust analysers on ESA's Rosetta mission, which was launched on 2 March 2004 [3]. The instrument was re-commissioned in April and July 2014 and operated next to the nucleus of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko from August 2014 to September 2016 [4]. Published parameters from the instrument paper are: mass 19.8 kg; power 20.4 W from a nominal 28 V DC spacecraft supply; atomic mass range 1 to 3500 amu; mass resolution m/Δm (50% peak width) above 2000 at 100 amu; 115In+ primary ions at 8 keV with a pulse duration of 3 ns; and a telemetry rate of about 500 bit/s [3]. The MPS summary page gives a mass resolution of about 1500 at 100 amu, which differs from the paper's value [4]. The retrieved text does not state external dimensions. The paper also lists, as a design requirement, an elliptical primary-beam focal spot with a major axis below 20 µm, while its overall parameter table gives a beam width of about 50 µm FWHM. The retrieved text does not reconcile these two statements [3]. The flight model comprised a dust funnel, a target manipulation unit (TMU) and primary indium ion sources [3]. Dust was collected onto electrically conducting targets, which the TMU positioned for analysis [3]. Two MPS images of the flight model and the TMU are shown below.
examples.power_supply: Nominal +28 V DC from the Rosetta spacecraft power subsystem [3]
examples.dimensions: External dimensions not stated in the sources accessed
examples.mass_resolution: m/Δm (50% peak width) > 2000 at m = 100 amu [3]; about 1500 at 100 amu on the MPS summary page [4] (discrepancy)
examples.primary_ion: 115In+, 8 keV, 3 ns pulses; beam width about 50 µm FWHM [3]; design requirement focal spot major axis < 20 µm [3]
examples.operations: Re-commissioned April and July 2014; operated near the nucleus August 2014 to September 2016 [4]

examples.name: Laboratory SIMS analysis of lunar volcanic glass beads (Saal et al. 2008)
examples.type: Laboratory SIMS instruments on Earth (Cameca IMS 6f ion probe and NanoSIMS 50L), applied to lunar samples [1]
examples.status: Laboratory instruments on Earth. Not flown in this role [1].
examples.description: **Status: laboratory instruments on Earth, applied to returned lunar samples [1].** Saal et al. used a Cameca IMS 6f ion probe and a NanoSIMS 50L for trace and volatile elements, and a Cameca SX100 electron microprobe for major elements [1]. For the IMS 6f measurement, the Cs+ primary beam was about 14 nA at 10 kV. The beam was rastered over a 25 µm area, producing a crater of about 35 µm [1]. Reported ranges across the glass beads are H2O 4 to 46 ppm, F 4 to 40 ppm, S 115 to 576 ppm and Cl 0.06 to 2 ppm. Essentially all volcanic glasses had CO2 within two standard deviations of the detection limit [1]. The Methods state trace-element precision better than 15% (2σ) [1]. The sample numbers used were 15427,41 (very-low-Ti and low-Ti glasses) and 74220,864 (high-Ti glasses), as listed in the paper [1]. Mass, dimensions and power of the instruments are not stated in the sources accessed. The modelled pre-eruptive water values (745 ppm best estimate; at least 260 ppm at 95% confidence) come from diffusion modelling, not from instrument output [1].
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed

examples.name: NanoSIMS analysis of olivine-hosted lunar melt inclusions (Hauri et al. 2011)
examples.type: Laboratory NanoSIMS on Earth, applied to lunar melt inclusions [2]
examples.status: Laboratory instrument on Earth. Not flown in this role [2].
examples.description: **Status: laboratory instrument on Earth, applied to lunar melt inclusions [2].** Hauri et al. measured water in melt inclusions, which are small pockets of magma sealed inside olivine crystals before eruption. The abstract reports that these crystal hosts limited water loss during eruption, so the values reflect pre-eruptive magma [2]. The abstract reports 615 to 1410 ppm water, with correlated fluorine, sulfur and chlorine [2]. Press coverage attributes the analyses to a NanoSIMS 50L on seven inclusion samples from Apollo 17 sample 74220. This was not verified against the full paper, which could not be accessed, so it is stated here only as a reported detail. Mass, dimensions and power are not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed
examples.instrument_reported_secondary_only: NanoSIMS 50L (press coverage, not verified in full text)

examples.name: Solar-wind-induced SIMS measurement concept (Elphic et al. 1991)
examples.type: Proposed lunar surface measurement concept with laboratory support; no lunar instrument specified [5]
examples.status: Concept and laboratory study. Not flown [5].
examples.description: **Status: proposed measurement concept with laboratory support. No flown or specified lunar instrument [5].** Elphic et al. examined whether solar-wind ions striking the lunar surface produce measurable secondary ions. The retrieved abstract describes solar-wind ions of about 95% H+ and 5% He++ bombarding the surface and sputtering atoms and secondary ions from the regolith [5]. The authors report that H+ and He++, although not efficient sputterers, produce significant fluxes of secondary lunar ions, including Na+, Mg+, Al+, Si+, K+, Ca+, Ti+, Mn+ and Fe+ [5]. They also predict fluxes of roughly 10 to 10,000 ions per cm² per second, depending on species [5]. These are predictions, not measurements from a lunar instrument. The retrieved summary indicates that the laboratory work used lunar soil simulants; this was not confirmed in the full text. No instrument mass, dimensions, power or sensitivity is given in the retrieved text, so these are not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for a SIMS payload. The only published spacecraft-level dimensions in the sources accessed are unstated for COSIMA [3][4]; the laboratory instruments and the concept have no dimensions stated in the sources accessed. Any lunar SIMS would need its dimensions set by its ion source, analyser, vacuum system, sample-handling interface and mounting, none of which has been specified.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: COSIMA's published mass is 19.8 kg [3]. Laboratory SIMS masses and any lunar SIMS mass are not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: COSIMA's published power draw is 20.4 W from a nominal 28 V DC spacecraft supply [3]. Power for the laboratory instruments and for any lunar SIMS is not publicly specified in the sources accessed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The lunar surface is a demanding environment for any mass spectrometer. The NASA Moon Fact Sheet gives an equatorial diurnal temperature range of 95 K to 390 K and a surface gravity of 1.62 m/s² [6]. NASA's Moon facts page states that the surface reaches about 127 °C in full sun and about -173 °C in darkness [7]. It also describes the lunar atmosphere as very thin and weak, providing no protection from solar radiation or meteoroid impacts [7]. A surface SIMS would therefore need thermal control, radiation-tolerant electronics and mechanical protection from dust and impacts, as well as a stable vacuum for its ion beam and detector. These requirements are general engineering reasoning rather than figures from the cited sources. No lunar-specific environmental requirement has been published for a SIMS in the sources accessed. For the flown COSIMA example, the instrument drew a nominal 28 V DC supply from the spacecraft [3]. Environmental qualification levels are not stated in the sources accessed.
article.limitations: The main limitation of this payload class is that SIMS is established in laboratories and in one spacecraft flight at a comet, but has not been confirmed on the Moon. A surface instrument would need regolith samples delivered in a form suitable for analysis. COSIMA's solution was a dust funnel and target manipulator that collected grains onto conducting targets [3]; no equivalent lunar sample interface has been specified. Each analysis also consumes sample material, as the crater size in the laboratory example shows [1]. Results depend on calibration, sample mounting and sample history. Saal et al. had to show that the water they measured was indigenous rather than solar-wind implanted or introduced in the laboratory [1]. Published mass resolution and beam size values for COSIMA differ between sources [3][4].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: No lunar SIMS has been verified for delivery to the surface. This section therefore describes the requirements a future surface payload would have to meet, not a specific mission.
transportation_process: Integrate the SIMS on Earth into a lander or rover payload, with its sample-handling, vacuum and thermal interfaces defined.
Launch the lander or rover on a launch vehicle and transfer it towards the Moon.
Land the payload and deploy the SIMS and its sample-handling system on the surface.
Deliver regolith to the analyser through a sample-acquisition interface, then run the analysis sequence.
Connect power, data and thermal control; the COSIMA example illustrates the scale of such interfaces, with a 28 V supply, 20.4 W power draw and about 500 bit/s telemetry [3].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: A future surface SIMS would need a sample-acquisition and presentation method, because the analyser must receive a prepared surface or grains on a conducting target. COSIMA used a dust funnel and target manipulation unit for this purpose [3]. No lunar deployment method has been specified for a SIMS.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: COSIMA was integrated into the Rosetta orbiter, which was launched on 2 March 2004, and operated at the comet from 2014 to 2016 [3][4]. This example shows spacecraft integration and operation at a comet. It does not show lunar transfer or landing.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with any named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. A future assessment would need verified mass, dimensions, mounting, sample-handling, power and data interfaces. None of these is available for a lunar SIMS in the sources accessed.

article.historical_significance: SIMS has two main lines of historical significance here. In lunar science, the Saal et al. study changed the debate about lunar water by reporting what its authors described as the first evidence for indigenous water in the lunar interior [1]. The Hauri et al. study reported higher water contents in melt inclusions than earlier direct glass measurements had shown [2]. In planetary exploration, COSIMA was one of three cometary dust analysers on ESA's Rosetta mission, and it demonstrated SIMS operation in space at a comet [3][4]. No lunar in-situ SIMS is recorded in the sources accessed.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
This article draws on three kinds of evidence, and it should be read with those categories in mind: flown hardware (COSIMA), laboratory analysis of lunar samples (Saal et al. 2008 and Hauri et al. 2011) and a proposed measurement concept (Elphic et al. 1991). None of the lunar evidence comes from an instrument on the Moon.

No lunar SIMS was found. Searches for SIMS payloads on lunar landers and rovers, including Chinese and Indian lunar programmes, returned no verified instrument. This is a limit of the sources accessed, not proof that no such instrument exists.

COSIMA specification values differ between sources. The paper gives mass resolution above 2000 at 100 amu, while the MPS summary gives about 1500 [3][4]. The paper also gives both a beam-width figure of about 50 µm FWHM and a design requirement of a focal spot below 20 µm major axis [3]. External dimensions are not stated in the retrieved text.

The Saal et al. text was retrieved from a PDF whose unit symbols were partly unreadable. Crater and beam sizes were read as micrometres (µm). These should be checked against the original paper [1].

The full text of Hauri et al. could not be accessed. The 615 to 1410 ppm range and the 50 ppm comparison come from the abstract summary, and the instrument and sample count come from secondary press coverage [2].

The full text of Elphic et al. was not accessed. Its laboratory details (simulants) and flux predictions come from the abstract summary and should be checked against the paper [5].

The two COSIMA images are from an MPS project page. Identification relies on the page captions, and rights are held by MPE and MPE/CEMEC, so reuse requires permission [4].

The environmental figures come from NASA sources last updated in January 2024 (NSSDC) and February 2026 (NASA facts page) [6][7]. The 745 ppm and 260 ppm water values are model results, not measurements [1]. Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.

data_quality_notes: No secondary ion mass spectrometer has been confirmed as flown, operating or formally planned on the Moon in the sources accessed. Searches of Chinese and Indian lunar programme payloads and general lunar in-situ mass spectrometry returned no SIMS instrument.
COSIMA (Rosetta) is a flown SIMS but flew to a comet, not the Moon. It is included only as the flight-heritage example for the technique.

COSIMA mass resolution differs by source: above 2000 at 100 amu in the instrument paper [3] versus about 1500 at 100 amu on the MPS summary page [4]. The paper's own beam description (design requirement of a focal spot under 20 µm major axis versus overall beam width of about 50 µm FWHM) is not reconciled in the retrieved text. External dimensions are not stated.
The COSIMA instrument paper's journal reference, volume and publication date were not confirmed in the retrieved text. The reference is cited by title and PDS archive URL.

Saal et al. (2008): the full text was retrieved from a scanned PDF whose unit symbols were partly unreadable. Crater and beam sizes were read as micrometres; this should be checked against the original paper. Mass, dimensions and power of the IMS 6f and NanoSIMS 50L instruments are not stated in the sources accessed.

Saal et al. (2008): the 745 ppm best estimate and 260 ppm minimum are diffusion-model results, not measurements. The paper's detection-limit improvement is stated qualitatively (up to two orders of magnitude); no numeric detection limit was verified.

Hauri et al. (2011): the full paper could not be accessed (publisher page returned HTTP 403). The 615 to 1410 ppm water range and the approximately 50 ppm comparison are from the abstract summary retrieved via the NCBI E-utilities record. The NanoSIMS 50L instrument, the seven inclusion samples and the Apollo 17 sample 74220 attribution come from secondary press coverage and are not verified against the full paper.

Elphic et al. (1991): only the abstract summary was retrieved. Laboratory details (lunar soil simulants) and the flux prediction (roughly 10 to 10,000 ions per cm² per second) are from that summary and are not verified against the full text. Instrument specifications are not publicly specified in the sources accessed.

Images: two COSIMA images (flight model and TMU) from the MPS COSIMA project page. Each cleaned URL (query string removed) was fetched and returned image/jpeg, and both images were viewed. Identification relies on the MPS alt text and captions. Rights are held by MPE and MPE/CEMEC; reuse requires permission. No lunar or laboratory SIMS image has a verified direct asset URL, so none is included.

Environmental values: equatorial diurnal range and surface gravity from the NSSDC Moon Fact Sheet (last updated 11 January 2024) [6]; surface temperature in full sun and darkness and atmosphere statements from the NASA Moon facts page (last updated 12 February 2026 as shown) [7]. The two sources differ in presentation and were not reconciled into one table.

PROSPECT (ref 8): instrument technique (ion trap and magnetic sector mass spectrometers; no SIMS) is taken from the article text as summarised by the retrieval tool. Its authors were not confirmed in the retrieved text.
The lunar transportation and compatibility sections make no compatibility claim. No lander, rover or spacecraft interface for a lunar SIMS has been verified.
Technical specifications are not fully audited. The lunar surface environmental requirements for a SIMS are general engineering reasoning, not sourced requirements.
